title: Canva Shares S3 Based Architecture for Session Revocation Across Hundreds of Millions of Sessions
gist: Canva replaced MySQL-backed session revocation lookups with 16-byte immutable records stored in 30-minute Amazon S3 chunks, distributed to gateways as sorted in-memory arrays, cutting revocation cache memory 87.5% and shrinking its revocation database to two read replicas. The notable architectural move is using S3's conditional PUTs and immutable objects as coordination primitives in place of Redis or a dedicated datastore.

themes.theme: S3 as coordination substrate, not object store

insights.claim: Canva chose Amazon S3 over Redis for revocation data specifically to avoid operating another datastore while still getting durable storage, treating object storage as a substitute for a caching tier.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Operational-headcount avoidance is beating raw latency as the deciding factor in datastore selection — a structural headwind for standalone managed cache vendors.
insights.quote: Canva chose Amazon S3 over Redis to avoid operating another datastore while providing durable storage for revocation data.
insights.locator: Canva chose Amazon S3 over Redis

insights.claim: Conditional PUTs on S3 objects supply optimistic concurrency control when multiple asynchronous workers update the same revocation chunk, with ZooKeeper leader election used only to reduce conflicts and explicitly not required for correctness.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Correctness residing in S3's conditional writes rather than a consensus service means teams can delete coordination infrastructure — watch for ZooKeeper/etcd footprint shrinking in similar designs.
insights.quote: Conditional PUTs provide optimistic concurrency control when workers update the same object, while ZooKeeper leader election reduces conflicts but is not required for correctness.
insights.locator: Asynchronous workers scan for new revocations

insights.claim: Software engineer Adam Urban, sharing the piece on LinkedIn, framed the design's significance as S3 being used as more than an object store, with immutable objects and conditional writes serving as coordination primitives.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Practitioner consensus forming around S3-as-coordination-layer expands AWS's moat beyond storage into distributed-systems primitives.
insights.quote: pointing to its use of immutable objects and conditional writes as coordination primitives

themes.theme: Compact binary encoding as the memory lever

insights.claim: Each revocation is encoded as a 16-byte binary record containing a principal and a timestamp, held in sorted arrays that allow direct in-memory search — a representation change that cut the revocation cache footprint by 87.5%.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: An 87.5% memory reduction from encoding alone shows data-representation work still yields order-of-magnitude infrastructure savings without new hardware or vendors.
insights.quote: Each revocation is represented as a 16-byte binary record containing a principal and timestamp. Sorted arrays enable direct in-memory searches, reducing the cache footprint by 87.5%.

insights.claim: At 16 bytes per record, a chunk holding one million revocations is only about 16 megabytes of binary data, making full-state transfer over the network cheap enough to be routine.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: When the entire revocation universe fits in tens of megabytes, the case for a networked lookup on the hot path largely disappears.
insights.quote: even a chunk containing one million revocations represents about 16 megabytes of binary data
insights.locator: Canva said the worker can process

insights.claim: The 12-hour revocation window is partitioned into 30-minute S3 objects that gateways fetch via conditional GETs, downloading only changed chunks and discarding data older than 12 hours.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Time-bucketed immutable chunks plus conditional GETs is a reusable pattern for pushing any bounded-window dataset to fleet edges without a database.

themes.theme: Deployment thundering herd as the forcing function

insights.claim: The original design failed because hundreds of gateway instances could each request more than a million revocations from MySQL during a deployment, producing coordinated database load that scaled with fleet size rather than with user activity.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Cache-warming on deploy is an under-modeled scaling failure mode: database load tied to instance count, not traffic, breaks as fleets grow.
insights.quote: hundreds of gateway instances could each request more than a million revocations from MySQL during deployments, creating a coordinated database load
insights.locator: As the platform grew, hundreds of gateway instances

insights.claim: After migration, database load became predictable because it now scales with revocation write throughput and overall site traffic rather than with the number of gateway instances loading the cache.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Decoupling backend load from fleet size is the durable win — it removes a scaling ceiling on horizontal expansion.
insights.quote: scaling with revocation write throughput and overall site traffic rather than the number of gateway instances loading the cache

insights.claim: Canva reduced its session revocation database to just two read replicas kept for redundancy and improved deployment speed following the migration.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that object-storage-backed designs can retire most of a relational fleet — relevant to database licensing and RDS spend forecasts.

insights.claim: A gateway can reconstruct its entire local revocation state by downloading the relevant S3 chunks, removing the database from the disaster-recovery and cold-start path altogether.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Recovery independence from the primary database materially changes the blast radius of a database outage for authentication.
insights.locator: The design also addresses recovery and deployment

themes.theme: Pushback: refresh tokens versus in-memory revocation

insights.claim: A Reddit commenter argued the whole design is unnecessary — short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens held in a database would avoid checking each session against a million cached revocations.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The standard-practice alternative exists and is cheaper to build; the fact that Canva rejected it signals where the real constraint lies.
insights.quote: Just use a refresh token scheme, keep access token lifetimes short and keep refresh tokens in a database instead, no need to check each session against a million cached revocations.
insights.locator: The architecture prompted discussion on Reddit

insights.claim: Canva engineer Llew Vallis defended in-memory revocation on the grounds that frequent token refreshes would increase database load and make availability dependent on the database during refresh operations.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The trade is availability coupling, not compute: at Canva's scale a refresh-token scheme makes login availability a function of database uptime.
insights.quote: Keeping revocation data in memory provided better tradeoffs because frequent token refreshes would increase database load and make availability dependent on the database during refresh operations.

insights.claim: Canva stores session information in encrypted browser cookies so gateways can authenticate requests without contacting a networked datastore, making revocation propagation the only remaining reason to touch a backend on the auth path.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Stateless cookie auth only fully pays off once revocation is solved locally — this is the missing piece that makes the pattern viable at hundreds of millions of sessions.
insights.locator: Canva stores session information in encrypted browser cookies

insights.claim: Asynchronous workers scanning for new revocations can process more than 2,000 revocations per second, which Canva says exceeds its expected requirements.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Headroom above requirement at 2,000/sec suggests the design is not near its ceiling — the pattern likely generalizes to larger fleets.
insights.locator: Canva said the worker can process

insights.claim: Canva credits testing multiple implementations on real infrastructure — including workloads with hundreds of thousands of revocations in a single array — for validating that the chosen design met scalability requirements.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Bake-off-on-production-infrastructure as a design methodology is the differentiator here, not the S3 trick itself.
